take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a

every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications with a `ponytail:` comment (`// ponytail: this exists`), simple reads as intent, not ignorance. Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

# HEARD Research & Launch Strategy

**Evidence base and LinkedIn launch playbook for HEARD: a platform connecting isolated individuals with trained peer listeners from underemployed populations (blind, disabled, elderly, and displaced people).**

`Status: Active Research & Launch Planning` · `Phase: Pre-Launch`

> **Live platform:** [heard.teww.org](https://heard.teww.org)
> **Related Application:** [heard-backup](https://github.com/Taha-Mahmoodi/heard-backup) — the HEARD platform codebase, built on this same research.

---

## Contents

- **[HEARD_Launch_Campaign.md](HEARD_Launch_Campaign.md)** — the original research document, verbatim: verified statistics, LinkedIn best practices, all 11 posts, and the posting calendar
- **[docs/STATISTICS.md](docs/STATISTICS.md)** — the same statistics, split out one-per-entry with source and verification notes
- **[docs/POSTS.md](docs/POSTS.md)** — the 11 posts, split out for easy copy-paste
- **[docs/LINKEDIN_STRATEGY.md](docs/LINKEDIN_STRATEGY.md)** — the LinkedIn best-practices section, expanded with structure/formatting notes

The three docs are the same content as the source document, reorganized for readability — nothing in them should say anything the source doesn't already say. If you spot something that does, flag it, that's a bug in the split.

---

## What Is HEARD? (from the source doc's TL;DR)

The evidence base for HEARD centers on two anchors: the WHO's June 2025 estimate that loneliness contributes to ~871,000 deaths a year, and the US Surgeon General's May 2023 advisory equating social disconnection with smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day.

On blind employment, the honest framing is that about 44% of working-age Americans with vision loss are employed versus 77% of people without disabilities — not the unsupported "70% unemployment" figure, which the National Research and Training Center on Blindness and Low Vision calls a myth. Remote work is the single biggest recent driver of disability employment gains, which is HEARD's core argument for building a remote-first listener workforce.

---

## Platform, Verified (heard.teww.org, checked July 2026)

The source doc's caveat that the platform "could not be independently verified" is now resolved — the live site confirms:

- **Voice-first, not text/chat.** Listeners record a short voice intro; callers pick who to talk to by how they sound, not a profile or photo.
- **Call structure:** 15, 30, or 45-minute conversations, caller's choice.
- **Traction so far:** 1,000+ calls answered, 200 blind & low-vision listeners, 11 languages (Dari, Pashto, Persian, Arabic & more).
- **Non-clinical framing is already explicit on-site:** "Companionship and conversation — never therapy."
- **Crisis resources are already built in** — a 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline link and a 911 emergency notice are present on the page. This closes the gap the source doc flagged ("consider adding a crisis-resources note").
- **Listener recruitment is live**, pitched specifically at blind/visually impaired people: "flexible, voice-only work built to be operated entirely by screen reader and keyboard."

This means Posts 4-9, which describe listener recruitment and the peer-support model, are describing a real, shipped mechanic — not a plan. One correction for the posts: they're written around "talk to a listener" in general terms; the actual product is voice-call based, which the posts don't contradict but also don't specify. Worth deciding whether to make "voice" explicit in the copy before publishing.

## Remaining Caveats (from the source doc)

- **Do not use the "70% unemployment" figure.** It's explicitly labeled a myth. Use "about 44% employed vs. 77%" instead.
- **Founder biography** (Posts 1 and 11 assume the founder is blind and describe a personal origin story) — still worth confirming this is literally true before publishing under the founder's name.
- **Refugee loneliness figures are ranges** from a systematic review, not single national statistics — keep them phrased as ranges.
- **The WHO 871,000-deaths figure is an estimate covering 2014-2019**, per The Lancet Public Health. Cite it as "the WHO estimates."

---

## Contributing

If you find additional sources, spot an outdated statistic, or have field feedback from HEARD users, open an issue or PR.

---

1	# HEARD Launch Campaign: Verified Statistics, LinkedIn Playbook, and 11 Ready-to-Post Founder-Voice Posts
2	
3	## TL;DR
4	
5	The evidence base for HEARD is strong, current, and citable. The WHO's June 30, 2025 Commission on Social Connection links loneliness to approximately 871,000 deaths per year (about 100 an hour), and the US Surgeon General's May 2023 advisory equates social disconnection with smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day. These two anchors alone justify the entire mission.
6	
7	On blind employment, use the honest, defensible framing, not the shaky "70%" myth. Only about 44% of working-age Americans with vision loss are employed versus 77% of people without disabilities (National Research and Training Center on Blindness and Low Vision), and remote work is the single biggest recent driver of disability employment gains, which is HEARD's core argument.
8	
9	On LinkedIn in 2025-2026, post 3 to 4 times a week in the founder's voice. Lead with a strong first line, keep posts near 800 to 1000 characters, use 3 to 5 hashtags, put links in the first comment, and reply fast in the first hour. The 11 drafted posts below are ready to publish as-is (no em dashes).
10	
11	---
12	
13	## KEY FINDINGS: Verified Statistics With Named Sources
14	
15	Verify each against the named source before publishing. All are from 2023-2026 sources except where a foundational study is noted.
16	
17	### 1. The loneliness and isolation epidemic
18	
19	**US Surgeon General, "Our Epidemic of Loneliness and Isolation," May 2023:** lacking social connection is "as dangerous as smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day." (NPR) Poor social connection is associated with a 29% increased risk of heart disease, a 32% increased risk of stroke, and a 50% increased risk of dementia in older adults.
20	
21	**WHO Commission on Social Connection, "From loneliness to social connection," June 30, 2025:** "New estimates suggest that loneliness accounts for approximately 871,000 deaths each year, or around 100 deaths an hour." The report states 1 in 6 people worldwide are affected by loneliness. (The Lancet Public Health notes the estimate covers the period 2014-2019.) Social isolation affects up to 1 in 3 older adults and 1 in 4 adolescents. (WHO)
22	
23	**American Psychological Association, "Stress in America" 2025 survey** (released Nov 6, 2025; Harris Poll, 3,199 US adults): "half or more adults said they felt isolated (54%), left out (50%) or lacking companionship (50%) often or some of the time," (APA) and "nearly seven in 10 (69%) said they needed more emotional support in the past year than they received, an increase from 65% in 2024."
24	
25	**American Psychiatric Association Healthy Minds poll, January 2024:** 30% of US adults said they felt lonely at least once a week; 10% said they felt lonely every day.
26	
27	### 2. Blind and visually impaired employment
28	
29	The "70% unemployment" figure is contested and should be avoided as a hard stat. The National Research and Training Center on Blindness and Low Vision (Mississippi State University) explicitly calls it a myth. Using national data (McDonnall & Sui summary; 2023 American Community Survey, ages 18-64): "about 44% of the U.S. population with a visual impairment were employed and 10% were unemployed. This compares to a 77% employment rate and 5% unemployment rate for people without disabilities." (Msstate) The real story is low labor-force participation, not the technical unemployment rate.
30	
31	**Use this framing:** "Only about 44% of working-age blind adults are employed, versus about 77% of people without disabilities."
32	
33	### 3. General disability employment and remote work
34	
35	**US Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2024:** the employment-population ratio for people with a disability reached a series high of 22.7%; the unemployment rate for people with a disability was 7.5%, roughly twice the rate for people without disabilities.
36	
37	**BLS, 2024:** about 25% of workers with a disability teleworked, slightly higher than the 23% of workers without disabilities.
38	
39	**Bloom, Dahl & Rooth, NBER Working Paper No. 32943 (2024), via CEPR/VoxEU:** working from home drove "a rise in employment of approximately a quarter of a million people across the US by 2024 alone," explaining 68% to 85% of the rise in full-time employment among people with physical disabilities post-COVID.
40	
41	### 4. Elderly isolation and reminiscence
42	
43	**University of Michigan National Poll on Healthy Aging, 2024** (published in JAMA): 33% of adults aged 50 to 80 felt lonely and 29% felt isolated in the past year.
44	
45	**Gardiner et al. meta-analysis:** roughly 61% of older people in care homes may be moderately lonely and about 35% severely lonely. (Altarum)
46	
47	**Reminiscence therapy:** a 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis in Frontiers in Psychiatry found a medium-to-large effect (SMD -0.61) on reducing depressive symptoms in older adults without significant cognitive impairment.
48	
49	### 5. Refugees and displaced people
50	
51	**Nguyen et al., 2024 systematic review, Social Science & Medicine:** among refugees resettled in high-income countries, loneliness prevalence ranged from 15.9% to 47.7% and social isolation from 9.8% to 61.2%, higher than population norms.
52	
53	**Côté-Olijnyk et al., 2024 meta-analysis** (cited by US Committee for Refugees and Immigrants): among asylum seekers and undocumented migrants in indefinite waiting, over a third experienced PTSD, over a third an anxiety disorder, and about half experienced depression.
54	
55	### 6. Peer support and being heard
56	
57	**Cooper et al., 2024 umbrella review, BMC Medicine:** consistent evidence that paid peer support improves outcomes such as hope, empowerment, and recovery for people with mental health challenges (though effects on clinical symptoms are mixed, so frame peer support as connection and hope, not treatment).
58	
59	**Marmalade Trust Loneliness Awareness Week 2025 Impact Report:** "96% of respondents felt 'quite' or 'extremely connected' after taking part," (Marmalade Trust) and 87% "said they had started a conversation with someone new about loneliness during the week." (Connexion Blog)
60	
61	---
62	
63	## LINKEDIN BEST PRACTICES (2025-2026)
64	
65	**Cadence:** Buffer's analysis of 2M+ posts across 94,000 accounts found 2 to 5 posts per week is the sweet spot, delivering roughly 1,182 more impressions per post and a 0.23-point engagement lift over posting once a week. For a founder building a narrative, 3 to 4 high-quality posts a week is ideal.
66	
67	**Founder voice vs org page:** Personal founder profiles massively outperform organic company-page posts (several 2025 analyses note organic company-page reach is now minimal). Strategy: publish from the founder's profile, then have the Third Eye Worldwide page reshare within a few hours, and have one or two team members add a genuine comment. Employee and supporter reshares multiply reach into trusted networks. (MechaBee)
68	
69	**Timing:** Buffer's 2026 data shows strong performance Tuesday and Wednesday mornings (8 to 9am) with late afternoon and evening (3 to 8pm) rising; Sprout Social recommends Tuesday to Thursday, 10am to 4pm for nonprofits. Consistency of timing matters more than the exact slot.
70	
71	**Structure:** Keep posts near 800 to 1000 characters (roughly 150 to 250 words). The first one or two lines are the only thing visible before "see more," so the hook must land there. Use short paragraphs and white space. End with one clear call to action plus a question to spark comments.
72	
73	**Format:** Document carousels (highest engagement, around 6.6%) and native video perform best, but strong text posts still work when hook and story are compelling. Put external links in the first comment, not the body, and remove link preview cards (links in body reduce reach).
74	
75	**Hashtags:** Use 3 to 5 per post, mixing one broad tag with two or three niche tags, placed at the end. More than five can trigger spam filtering (some analyses cite a large reach penalty). Note: hashtag impact on discovery has weakened; they now function more like SEO keywords.
76	
77	**Algorithm:** The 2025-2026 feed is relevance-driven and rewards dwell time and thoughtful comments over likes. The first 60 to 120 minutes determine reach trajectory, so reply quickly. (Authoredup) Avoid engagement bait ("comment YES") and formulaic AI-sounding content, both of which are downranked. Evergreen, high-value posts now resurface for weeks.
78	
79	---
80	
81	## THE 11 READY-TO-POST LINKEDIN POSTS
82	
83	*(First-person founder voice. No em dashes. Each has a hook, short body, CTA, and 3-5 hashtags.)*
84	
85	### Post 1 — Founder story and origin
86	
87	I am blind. For a long time, the world decided that meant I had nothing to offer.
88	
89	I built HEARD to prove the opposite.
90	
91	HEARD is a platform where people who feel isolated can talk to a real human being who will actually listen. And the listeners are people the job market too often ignores: blind people, disabled people, elderly people, and people who have been displaced from their homes.
92	
93	Here is what I learned living without sight. When you cannot rely on a glance across a room, you learn to listen for what people actually mean. That is not a disability. That is a skill. It is maybe the most human skill there is.
94	
95	So we decided to build a company around it.
96	
97	If you have ever felt unseen, or unheard, or written off, this is for you. Follow along. We are just getting started.
98	
99	`#Accessibility #DisabilityInclusion #SocialImpact #Loneliness #Startups`
100	
101	### Post 2 — The loneliness epidemic
102	
103	Loneliness is not just a feeling. It is a health crisis.
104	
105	The World Health Organization reported this year that loneliness is linked to around 871,000 deaths every year. That is about 100 people every hour.
106	
107	Let that sit for a second.
108	
109	We treat loneliness like a personal failing, something you should just get over. But the US Surgeon General has said that being socially disconnected is as dangerous as smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day.
110	
111	We would never tell someone to just get over a habit that deadly. So why do we say it about loneliness?
112	
113	At HEARD, we believe the answer to disconnection is connection. A real conversation with a real person who is fully present.
114	
115	That is the whole idea. That is the whole company.
116	
117	If this resonates, share it so more people see it.
118	
119	`#Loneliness #MentalHealth #SocialConnection #PublicHealth #HEARD`
120	
121	### Post 3 — Blind and disabled unemployment
122	
123	Here is a number that should bother you more than it does.
124	
125	Only about 44% of working-age Americans who are blind or have serious vision loss are employed. For people without disabilities, it is about 77%. That comes from the National Research and Training Center on Blindness and Low Vision.
126	
127	The problem was never ability. The problem was access.
128	
129	When work moved remote, something quietly incredible happened. Employment for disabled people hit record highs. Researchers found that working from home added more than a quarter of a million disabled workers to full-time jobs in the US alone.
130	
131	Flexibility is not a perk. For millions of us, it is the difference between a paycheck and poverty.
132	
133	HEARD is built remote-first, on purpose. Our listeners work from home, on their terms, and get paid for a genuinely human skill.
134	
135	Know a company that gets this? Tag them.
136	
137	`#DisabilityEmployment #RemoteWork #Accessibility #InclusiveHiring #FutureOfWork`
138	
139	### Post 4 — Call for the first listeners to join
140	
141	We are hiring our first listeners. And I could not be prouder of who we are looking for.
142	
143	If you are blind, disabled, elderly, or rebuilding your life after being displaced, and you are the person friends always come to when they need to talk, I want to hear from you.
144	
145	Here is what the job is. You listen. You are present. You hold space for someone who feels alone. You get paid to do it.
146	
147	Here is what the job is not. It is not therapy. It is not a call center with a script. It is not charity.
148

Verify each against the named source before publishing. All are from 2023-2026 sources except where a foundational study is noted.

### 1. The loneliness and isolation epidemic

**US Surgeon General, "Our Epidemic of Loneliness and Isolation," May 2023:** lacking social connection is "as dangerous as smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day." (NPR) Poor social connection is associated with a 29% increased risk of heart disease, a 32% increased risk of stroke, and a 50% increased risk of dementia in older adults.
